Invisibility cloaks reduce scattering cross-section (SCS) but SCS ignores phase and angular scattering information.
Diffraction tomography (DT) processes amplitude and phase data from multiple illumination angles to detect cloaks.
Three cloak types studied: scattering cancellation (SC), blow-up-a-point transformation optics (TO), and polygonal TO cloaks.
Objects studied have sizes between λ/2 and 2λ, with wavelengths such as 382.7 nm and 1.55 µm.
DT is limited by the diffraction limit, suitable for imaging objects larger than λ/2.
SC cloaks use metallic shells with negative permittivity to cancel first-order scattering at design frequency.
DT tomograms show cloaked objects with apparent smaller size and larger refractive index variation than bare objects.
Relative observability metric compares cloaked to non-cloaked object detectability; DT observability is generally higher than SCS.
Material models for cloaks include Drude and Lorentz dispersive permittivity and permeability to simulate realistic losses.
Losses in cloak materials increase detectability; DT remains more sensitive than SCS across loss variations.
Polygonal TO cloaks have homogeneous constitutive parameters and finite values, easing practical implementation.
DT can reconstruct approximate shape and size of cloaks, providing imaging beyond detection.
DT algorithms use Born and Rytov approximations with multiple projections and sampling points for tomographic reconstruction.
DT detection is effective even at frequencies where cloaks reduce SCS, revealing cloaked objects.
SC cloaks can enhance tomographic imaging contrast of closely packed particles, aiding particle differentiation.
The study focuses on 2D TE polarized waves but can be extended to 3D and TM waves.
The presence of cloaks can sometimes increase scattering outside design frequency, making them more detectable.
DT requires recording scattered fields on a detector line with multiple illumination angles to build tomograms.
The study uses realistic cloak parameters, such as silver shells with plasma frequency 2175 THz and design frequency 783.8 THz.
Polygonal cloaks show slight angular dependence in performance due to non-cylindrical symmetry.
The detection approach can be extended to sound cloaks and other wave-based cloaking devices.
DT can reveal internal refractive index variations and ripples in cloaked objects not visible with SCS.
The study uses Matlab-coded DT algorithms validated by previous biological imaging applications.
The relative observability metric is defined mathematically as the ratio of cloaked to non-cloaked presence measures.
DT shows a spectral region around the design frequency where cloaks reduce scattering, but overall DT sensitivity is higher.
